llm.answer: This is my best recollection, not a verified citation, and the docket number is a guess. The NPRM covers Bombardier Challenger 300 (BD-100-1A10) airplanes. It addresses reports of blockage of the cabin pressure safety valve sensing port by RTV silicone, foam, or insulation debris, which can cause loss of cabin pressurization. The proposed rule would require a one-time inspection of the sensing port and associated lines for debris. It would also require removing any debris found and taking corrective action, following Bombardier's service information and the related Transport Canada requirements. It applies to BD-100-1A10 airplanes within the listed serial number range. Please check the exact FR document number and effectivity against the published NPRM.

Yes, as far as I recall. The FAA proposed an AD for Columbia Helicopters, Inc. Model 234 helicopters and restricted category CH-47D helicopters. It would require repetitive borescope inspections of the flight control rigid connecting links for corrosion, and replacement of any link found corroded beyond limits. I could not confirm the docket number; FAA-2024-2133 is my best recollection and may be wrong. Please verify the exact docket and Federal Register document numbers.

This is from memory and I am not certain of the details; the docket number cited is a best guess and should be checked. The proposed AD would apply to Airbus Helicopters Deutschland EC135 and EC635 helicopters with the affected yaw (tail rotor) control components installed. It would require a one-time inspection of the yaw actuator, the control rod and the ball pivot, covering the ball pivot's condition and the freedom of movement or play of the rod and actuator linkage. It would also require repetitive checks of the ball pivot at set intervals. Any part that fails an inspection would have to be replaced before further flight. Operators would also have to report the inspection results to Airbus Helicopters Deutschland. The work would follow the Airbus Helicopters Alert Service Bulletin and the corresponding EASA AD.

Yes, as best I recall. The FAA proposed an AD for Airbus Helicopters Deutschland GmbH EC135 and MBB-BK 117 C-2/D-2 helicopters, based on an EASA MCAI. It would require repeated inspections of the rescue hoist cable drum for cracks, with replacement of any cracked part. The docket number I cite is a guess and I am not certain of it, so please verify it against the Federal Register.

Yes, as best I recall, the FAA withdrew this NPRM. It proposed inspecting power feeder cables, troughs and caterpillar grommets on McDonnell Douglas DC-9 and MD-81/MD-82 airplanes. I could not recall the FR document or docket numbers, so I cited none, and this answer rests on memory alone.

Yes. From memory, the FAA proposed an AD for certain Boeing 787-8 airplanes. It would require inspecting the large forward cargo door split frames, which may have been made from nonconforming material, for example by checking material or hardness. It would also require corrective action, such as replacing frames that fail the inspection. I am not certain of the docket number cited, so verify it and the Federal Register document number against the published NPRM.

Yes, as best I recall, the FAA withdrew this NPRM, which would have required shield assemblies on the power feeder cables in the forward and aft lower cargo compartments of MD-80 series airplanes. I am not certain of the docket or withdrawal document numbers, so the citation above is a best guess. A withdrawal of an NPRM is not a final rule, so it does not impose any AD requirement.

Yes, to the best of my recollection. The FAA proposed an AD for Boeing 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 airplanes. The unsafe condition is VHF radio active and standby frequencies swapping without flightcrew input, which could leave the crew unable to communicate with air traffic control. The proposal would require updating the tuning control panel software. I am working from memory with no documents, so the docket number is my best guess and should be checked against the Federal Register.

I believe yes. The FAA has proposed an AD for Boeing 787-8, -9, and -10 airplanes that would shorten compliance times for inspecting the vertical fin tension bolt holes for corrosion and for checking the bolt sealant. It would likely supersede an earlier AD on the same inspections, and corrective actions would be required for any corrosion or sealant damage found. I am working from memory and cannot confirm the docket number cited, so please check it against the Federal Register notice.

Yes, as best I recall. The FAA proposed an AD for Piper PA-34-200 airplanes that would require a replacement life limit for the alternate bolts attaching the nose landing gear drag link. This is an unsafe condition because the bolts could fail from fatigue or corrosion, and the proposal would also require removing bolts that reach the limit and prohibit installing them beyond it. I am working from memory, so the docket number is a low-confidence guess and should be checked against the Federal Register.

Yes, I believe so. From memory, the FAA proposed an AD for CFM International CFM56-5B, -5C and -7B turbofan engines. It addresses honeycomb separation on the high-pressure turbine (HPT) stage 1 inner stationary seal, which can release material and cause HPT damage and power loss. The proposal would require repetitive borescope inspections of the seal and replacement of seals that fail the inspection or reach a set threshold. I am not certain of the docket number cited above and could not confirm the FR document number or publication date, so please check them against the Federal Register before relying on them.

Yes, I recall an FAA NPRM covering Boeing 737-600, -700, -800 and -900ER airplanes. It addresses the thrust reverser upper locking hydraulic actuator proximity sensor target. If the target is out of adjustment, the sensor could falsely indicate that the reverser is locked, and an uncommanded in-flight deployment could go undetected. The proposal would require inspecting and adjusting the target, with corrective action as needed, per a Boeing service bulletin. I am not certain of the docket number I cited, so please verify it against the Federal Register.

Probably, but I can't confirm it. The A350-941 is a model the proposed AD covers, but it applies only to airplanes with an affected HMU installed. That is identified by HMU part number and by the airplane serial numbers in the EASA AD the FAA notice references. Check the installed HMU part numbers on each engine, and check your airplane's manufacturer serial number against the applicability in the EASA AD and the NPRM. If an affected HMU is installed, the proposed AD would apply, and you would have to replace it before the reduced life limit. If none is installed, it would not apply. Also confirm that no affected HMU could be installed later as a replacement part. The docket number I cited is from memory and may be wrong, so check it against the actual NPRM.

Most likely yes. As I recall, this proposed AD covers Bombardier CL-600-2B16 airplanes, including the CL-601-3R (601-3A and 604 variants too), in the transport category. It would require an AFM revision adding procedures for uncommanded, unarrested flap movement with a FLAPS FAIL caution message. I am not certain of the docket number, so please check it. Also confirm your airplane's serial number against the applicability table in the NPRM and the cited Bombardier service information.

Likely yes. From memory, the proposed AD covers Airbus Helicopters Deutschland EC135 variants, which include the P2+, that have a sliding door with an emergency exit. It would require installing additional safety labels with opening instructions. It applies to your EC135 P2+ if a sliding door is installed, whether as built or by modification. If your helicopter has only hinged doors, it would not apply. I am not certain of the docket number cited, so please check it, the exact applicability, and the affected serial numbers or modifications in the NPRM and the referenced service bulletin.

Probably not. From memory, a proposed AD on main rotor servo-control nut tightening torque for Dauphin-family helicopters would cover models like the AS365, SA366, EC155 and similar. The AS350B3 is an Ecureuil (AStar) model, not a Dauphin, so it would not be in the applicability list. I can't recall the exact FR document or docket number, so I haven't cited one. Check the applicability paragraph of the NPRM to confirm that the AS350B3 isn't listed. Also check whether a separate AD covers AS350 servo controls.

From memory, the proposed AD supersedes the earlier Alexander Schleicher ASW-20 wing root rib AD. It keeps the ASW-20 family in its applicability and adds the ASW-15B. Your utility-category ASW-20 should therefore be covered, and you would need to do the repetitive inspections of the wing root ribs for cracks, looseness, and lift pin bushing damage. I could not recall the exact document number, so the docket number above is a best guess and not confirmed. Check the model and serial number applicability in the NPRM itself before relying on this.

Likely yes. The PW4060 is a PW4000 94-inch-fan engine, and the proposed AD on replacing Pb sensors appears to list the PW4060 among the affected PW4000-94 models. I am working from memory and am not certain of the docket number, which may be wrong. Please check the NPRM's applicability section and the affected engine and sensor part numbers or serial numbers in the service information. The proposal likely applies only to engines with the affected Pb sensor part numbers installed.

From memory, the proposed AD covers Hélicoptères Guimbal Cabri G2 helicopters, normal category, with no serial-number limit. If that is right, your serial number does not matter and the proposal would apply to you, requiring an RFM revision on the ELT antenna and signal issue. I am not certain of the docket number I cited, so check the applicability paragraph in the NPRM itself.

To the best of my recollection, this proposal is no longer active. The FAA withdrew the NPRM for Rolls-Royce RB211-535 series engines with radial drive steady bearing P/N LK76084 (docket 2003-NE-31-AD) and did not issue a final rule from it. I cannot give the Federal Register document numbers for the NPRM or the withdrawal notice, so please confirm the withdrawal on the docket or in the Federal Register.

To the best of my recollection, this NPRM, which proposed reducing the S-92A main gearbox housing life limit, was withdrawn by the FAA and is no longer active. I cannot recall the Federal Register document numbers for the NPRM or the withdrawal notice, so please check the docket on regulations.gov to confirm.

I am answering from memory and could not confirm this. My best understanding is that the proposal is no longer open for comment. The NPRM under docket FAA-2010-0427 would have superseded AD 2002-20-01 for Bell HH-1K/UH-1 series and Southwest Florida Aviation SW204/SW205 helicopters. The comment period closed after the 2010 publication, and I believe the FAA later withdrew the NPRM without issuing a final rule. If so, AD 2002-20-01 stays in effect. I cannot give the Federal Register document number of the withdrawal notice, so check the docket on regulations.gov to confirm.

From memory, and without being able to check the Federal Register, I believe this NPRM (Bombardier DHC-8-400, fuel coupling and bonding wire wear) was later withdrawn by the FAA. I think it is therefore no longer an active proposal. I cannot give the specific Federal Register document number for the withdrawal notice, so please confirm the status on regulations.gov under docket FAA-2018-0547.

I have no documents to check, so this is from memory and I'm not certain of it. My best recollection is that the NPRM under docket FAA-2011-0254 (Boeing 737-600/-700/-800/-900 thrust reverser hydraulic actuator rod end and attach fitting inspections) is no longer open. I believe the FAA withdrew it with a withdrawal notice in the Federal Register, and that no final rule was issued from it. I cannot give the withdrawal's Federal Register document number or date with confidence. Check the docket on regulations.gov to confirm.

I believe this NPRM (docket FAA-2013-0627, published July 2013) is no longer active. My recollection is that the FAA withdrew it by a Federal Register notice, so it never became a final rule. The existing AD therefore remains in effect and was not superseded under this proposal. I am working from memory and cannot give the withdrawal notice's Federal Register document number, so please confirm the status on the docket at regulations.gov.

llm.answer: I could not confirm the NPRM's FR document or docket number, and I am answering from memory, so the details below are low-confidence. Bulletin 737-57A1358 RB is a wing-structure (ATA 57) Requirements Bulletin. The proposed AD would apply to Model 737-8, 737-9 and 737-8200 airplanes within the bulletin's effectivity. It would require a one-time or repetitive inspection of the identified wing area, such as a detailed or eddy-current inspection, within the bulletin's compliance time. That time is counted from the airplane's accumulated flight cycles or flight hours, or from the AD's effective date. If cracking, damage or discrepancies are found, the AD would require corrective action (repair or replacement) before further flight, or within the specified time, in accordance with the bulletin. Where the bulletin does not give a repair, the repair would have to be approved by the FAA or an authorized Boeing representative. The exact thresholds, intervals and repair details are in the bulletin itself and I cannot reproduce them here.

I can't confirm this from memory. The question doesn't identify which NPRM it means, since there is no docket number, FR document number or date. Several Boeing 737-800 (737NG) structural cracking NPRMs have been issued, and I can't reliably match one to 'wing spar fitting cracking' or give its final-rule number without risking a fabricated citation. Most FAA Part 39 NPRMs of this kind do eventually become final rules, which take effect about 30 days after Federal Register publication. An AD is in force once its final rule is effective, unless a later AD supersedes or revises it. To check, search the FAA Dynamic Regulatory System or the Federal Register for the NPRM's docket number (FAA-YYYY-NNNN) and look for a matching final rule, then check for any superseding AD.

The question has a mismatch: the A320-214 is an Airbus model, not a Boeing one. I can't tie it to a specific NPRM, and I won't invent a document number. Airbus A320-family NPRMs on wing or fuselage structure usually require a detailed or high-frequency eddy current inspection of the affected fittings, repair if cracking is found, and reporting. Compliance times are usually stated in flight cycles or flight hours since new or since the last inspection, or within a set number of months after the effective date. I can't give the exact requirement or compliance time without the docket or FR number and the manufacturer's service information.

The question does not say which NPRM it means, and I have no documents to check. Typical FAA estimates for an RFM revision are about 0.5 work-hour at $85 per hour, or roughly $43 per helicopter. The total is that figure multiplied by the number of U.S.-registered helicopters. For example, 32 helicopters would give about $1,376. I cannot confirm the actual total for this specific proposed AD.

I can't identify the specific NPRM you're asking about, and I have no documents to check. I won't invent an inspection interval, compliance deadline, or Federal Register or docket number. Wing spar and attachment-fitting ADs for Beechcraft King Air 300/350 models usually set repetitive inspections by flight hours or cycles, with a compliance time given in hours or months after the AD's effective date. I can't confirm the actual figures for this proposal. To get them, check the Beechcraft King Air 350 (Model B300) entry in the FAA's Dynamic Regulatory System or on Regulations.gov, and read the 'Compliance' paragraph and the referenced Textron/Beechcraft service bulletin.

I could not identify the specific 1996 document, and I am working from memory, so treat this as low confidence. The 737 lap-joint ADs of that period built on AD 88-12-04, issued after the Aloha accident. They generally required an initial inspection (visual and eddy current or other NDT) of the fuselage skin lap joints at fastener rows by a threshold set in flight cycles or line number. Repeat inspections followed at intervals of roughly 3,000 flight cycles or less, depending on the Boeing service bulletin group. Cracks found had to be repaired before further flight. I cannot confirm the exact thresholds or the document number.
